title: The Young Black Stallion
full_review:
An Arab girl befriends a spirited steed who runs like the wind in director Simon Wincer's feel-good family adventure "The Young Black Stallion" (Disney). Based on the late Walter Farley's children's book series and shot in supersized Imax format, the film's breathtaking desert vistas evoke the panoramic splendor of David Lean, while its threadbare narrative is just plain lean.

The film is set in 1946 North Africa. Newcomer Biana Tamimi plays Neera, a plucky Bedouin lass returning home to her grandfather's house after waiting out World War II in safekeeping. While en route, her caravan is attacked by desert marauders. Neera escapes harm but is thrown from her camel and left alone amid the horizonless waves of sand. Soon after, she encounters a wild stallion colt, orphaned when horse rustlers captured his mother, which she names Shetan.

They quickly develop one of those girl-and-her-horse bonds essential for the film's emotional payoff. They may not have water or a map, but you just know from the first nose-to-nuzzle kiss that they will find their way back home and eventually into the winner's circle.

Needless to say, Neera does make it through the wasteland to the welcoming arms of her grandfather, Ben Ishak (Richard Romanus). Before the war, Ishak had been a wealthy horse breeder with much clout among the local Bedouin tribal chiefs. But hard times have reduced him to near-poverty and left his opulent oasis casbah in disrepair, forcing him to sell off his once-envied stable of steeds, including his prize mare (of whom -- surprise, surprise -- Shetan proves to be a scion).

When Neera suggests that she ride her fiery pitch-black pony in an important annual race in the hope of restoring her grandfather's reputation, Ishak responds with one of those well-intentioned prohibitions that will only make her preordained, against-all-odds victory taste all the sweeter.

After training in secret, the day of the big race arrives. This will usher in a happy ending for Neera with the pounding of hooves and a cloud of desert dust, proving that underneath her ebony equine's untamable spirit is the heart of a champion. Move over Seabiscuit, there is a new underdog-and-pony show in town: Meet Sheik-biscuit.

Conceived as a prequel to the superior 1979 crowd pleaser, "The Black Stallion," the film is handicapped by Wincer's overenthusiasm for wow-inducing desert landscapes at the expense of well-developed characters in which viewers can invest more than just a knee-jerk rooting interest. And though it doesn't take much horse sense to figure out that the decision to shoot the film in Imax was predicated by a desire to show off its advantages over smaller formats (namely size and scope), the characters are so sketchy that viewers' emotional attachment to them fades as quickly as footprints in the desert sand.

Nowhere is this more evident than in the character of Mansoor (Ali Al Ameri), the film's default villain -- a designation indicated only by his "bad guy" black turban. Neera's relationship with Ishak is given similar short shrift, as is her preparation for the big race, which is conveyed through a brief blink-and-you'll-miss-it montage. Conversely, Neera's exodus across the desert is documented through protracted, albeit stunningly photographed, sequences -- "Lawrence of Arabia"-style panning shots play better on jumbo Imax screens than talking heads.

Story and technology jump into the same saddle and break out of their narrative trot into a full-blown gallop during the climactic race, a heart-pounding contest across the treacherous Moroccan terrain. And though viewers can almost feel the hot North African wind on their face during the race, its photo-finish would have packed more of an emotional punch if the characters involved weren't as one-dimensional as desert mirages.

While Neera and Ishak's religion never really comes into play, the positive portrayal of Muslims as loving, family-oriented characters is a welcome relief to the all-too-common negative stereotypes, which usually caricature Arabs as Quran-thumping fanatics or bomb-strapped terrorists.

Despite what neigh-sayers -- oops, naysayers -- may think, "The Young Black Stallion" is a beautifully shot, if not wholly satisfying, family-friendly tale that will nevertheless win your heart -- if only by a nose.

The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-I -- general patronage. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is G -- general audiences.
